## Discussion and conclusion

These results support the idea that even a judicial system operating in highly authoritarian systems can have a restraining effect on electoral manipulation. A qualitative analysis of the text of the 225 cases on election fraud also shows that, throughout the late Medvedev and second Putin presidencies, the criminal justice system has acted to shield higher-ups from responsibility for even confirmed instances of election fraud; front-line agents occasionally take the fall, while the system itself continues to operate. The tension between the needs of the overall system\textemdash to continue to control electoral outcomes, to allow a modest level of judicial independence, and to legitimize the regime itself through apparent rule of law\textemdash and the risks faced by the weakest agents of the ruling party is apparent here.

A brief case study of Dagestan, an influential set of observations in the statistical analysis, also supports the general claims made above. The district where a severe penalty for election fraud was handed down by the court showed a significant decline in evidence of election fraud after the verdict. Similarly situated regions experienced a similar decline, while qualitatively different regions\textemdash perhaps home to agents from different patronage networks\textemdash show an increase in fraud. This result is in keeping with a model in which front-line agents, rather than higher-level decision makers, are a constraining factor in the delivery of election manipulation. Most importantly, it supports the claim that these agents take legal risk into account, even in a highly authoritarian and pro-regime region. 

While the overall conclusion of this book is pessimistic for the role of protest in deterring electoral manipulation, these findings do indicate an important alternative avenue for both future research and pro-democratic practice. The results in this chapter show that electoral falsification can be significantly restrained through legal risks. Authoritarian incumbents face a dilemma which opposition parties and independent civil society groups can attempt to exploit. Authoritarian governments have strong incentives to permit a degree of independence in the judicial system, especially when they deal with low-level actors. However, by permitting more independent courts, they also intensify the principal-agent problems inherent in illegal electoral manipulation. Independent judiciaries create "a uniquely independent institution with public access in the midst of an authoritarian state” [@ginsburg_rule_2008, p. 13].

Legal mobilization by pro-democracy groups can intensify this effect on election integrity. The literature on legal mobilization shows that litigants can have a variety of reasons to take their cases to court, even if they expect an unfavorable ruling [@mccannRightsWorkPay1994]. Opposition groups may bring an alleged violation to court as a form of protest [@dorLitigationPoliticalParticipation2006], to raise publicity [@dotanLegalDefeatsPolitical2005;@mccannRightsWorkPay1994], or to lobby for concessions from the incumbent [@chernykh2014]. For individual candidates, casting doubt on an election result in court can be a way of retaining political credibility for future races [@kerrElectoralRulingsPublic2021].  Such strategic litigation can be especially beneficial for opposition actors when the issue is a valence issue---like election fraud, or corruption---that the government cannot defend on the merits [@aydincakirJudicializationPoliticsElected2014]. Add to this the fact that even unsuccessful criminal procedures impose financial, reputational, and other social costs on election-manipulating agents, which can shift them out of the falsification business.

More vigorous election monitoring and legal mobilization, conducted at the local level, can therefore make it considerably more difficult for incumbents to falsify election results. While they can remain capable of recruiting agents to engage in less attributable forms of manipulation, like vote-buying, constraints on falsification make election-rigging far more costly and complicated for incumbents. Principal-agent problems are especially stark for vote-buying and voter pressure efforts, where brokers are more diverse and harder to monitor than election officials. Brokers and voters both have incentives to defect, pocketing resources intended for election-rigging while misleading their superiors in the patronage network. Such efforts also directly involve the public, potentially increasing the legitimacy cost of manipulation in ways that extend beyond protest risk. By limiting the availability of falsification, legal mobilization can improve election integrity directly and indirectly---by increasing the cost to incumbents of each manufactured vote. In times of resource constraint or elite divisions, such costs may enable genuine opposition breakthroughs.
